title: Boiler Maps
description: Indoor navigation app for Purdue buildings.
story: During the Spring semester of 2026, my talented friend group took a class called CS307 - Software Engineering in the hopes of creating a project together. The class was structured such that we had to use agile methodologies to build a meaningful software project. We also had to present it at the end of the semester.

After multiple ideation sessions, we settled on creating an indoor navigation system for Purdue University. Indoor navigation is a notoriously difficult problem, and we were determined to solve it. The team experimented with a variety of technologies, including magnetic fingerprinting, BLE beacons, and Wi-Fi triangulation. We ultimately settled on an approach that combined pedometer readings for navigation and magnetic fingerprinting for location caliberation.

This project was not only challenging because of the technical complexities, but also because of the amount of manual work involved. There would be nights of testing where we would have to walk up and down buildings for us to caliberate stride length, and figure out how to fine-tune the accuracy of our system. Drawing out floorplans, marking magnetic fingerprints, and testing the app in different buildings was a lot of work, but was the most rewarding part of the project as those aspects are what made it stand out. We ended up with a working prototype for indoor navigation inone building, and a functioning outdoor to indoor navigation transition.

As this project was divided into 3 sprints, each 3 weeks long, we were able to make significant progress towards our functional and non-functional goals. Some other highlights include - interactive tutorial upon launching the app, an internal application to help us with node creation for path displays, and a custom-built step counter that was more accurate than the phone's built-in pedometer.

My wonderful teammates - Daniel, Gabe, Neha, Tory, and I (Shreya) won't stop here! In the future, we wish to make all our components in-house, instead of using the Google Maps API so that we have free reign over indoor map designs and capabilities. We also want to explore using machine learning models to help us select the best navigation approach as mentioned for different situations.

title: barbielang
description: A simple block-based programming language for beginners.
story: Spring 2026 was a semester of many fun projects! For the InnovateHER hackathon (of which I was also a part of the organizing team during its launch in 2024), my teammates and I created a block-based programming language for beginners. The idea stemmed from my longtime wish to create a programming language that was fun, eye-catching for beginners and had a cool theme. I began programming through Khan Academy's JavaScript course, and what I loved most about it was that nothing was dumbed down because I was a beginner, instead it was just made fun via visuals and interactivity. I envisioned a similar experience for barbielang.

barbielang blends familiar block-based programming paradigms with a fun, Barbie-inspired theme. The language is designed to be intuitive and engaging, making it an ideal choice for beginners or experts who want to enjoy a playful coding experience.

The development process involved using the somewhat old, but widely used Blockly library for the frontend. We customized the barebone environment to fit our Barbie theme, and added features like a block code to python translator, output section and glittering trashcan. I will say, I was very impressed with the UI/UX. Each design choice was intentional and well thought out by the creative experts of our team - Suhani and Pooja. Kartavya and I focused on the interpreter architecture. The lexer converts raw text into tokens. Then a parser builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) from those tokens and uses operator precednce, expression parsing and statement parsing. The evaluator evaluates the AST and executes the code. My course knowledge from making a simple C compiler in my Computer Architeture class played a huge role in helping me form parallels and understand the basic design needed for our interpreter.
barbielang was an eye-catching project at the hackathon demos, and we were thrilled to win at the hackathon as well!

I envision barbielang inspiring young coders to explore programming in a fun and engaging way. In the future, I hope to create barbieworld, a place for barbielang coders to interact with each other, share their projects on a public gallery, and even have barbie coding competetions. I also proposed the idea of AI generating the UI for multiple different themes as per kids' interests, and I hope to explore that in the future as well!

title: C Shell
description: Custom shell in C built for my Systems Programming class.
story: Systems Programming and Computer Security have been two of my most rewarding classes at Purdue, mainly because they both had incredibly involved projects, and I LOVE getting my hands dirty with projects. In the Spring of 2025, I took Systems Programming with Prof. Gustavo Rodriguez-Rivera, who sparked in me an interest for low-level programming. The class featured projects like building a shell, memory allocator, and creating an HTTP server.

For the Shell project, we were first tasked with tokenizing and parsing words using lex and yacc. This helped us create a basic command table. Then we had to execute the commands by creating a new process with fork() and calling the built-in library function execvp(). File and pipe redirection using dup2() was also part of the first milestone.

The second milestone involved adding support for signal handling (ctrl-c), builtin functions (cd, setenv, source), background processes, and subshells. The final milestone was to add support for environment variable expansion (${SHELL}, ${$}, ${!}, etc.), wildcards, command history, and tty controls

The hardest part of this project was definitely subshells and tty controls. The shell project made way more sense once I became a teaching assistant for the class. Looking at others' implementations also made me appreciate the use of C++ to simplify some string manipulation and memory management aspects of the project.
